lesson.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap
lesson.goal: build a command-line tool in Rust with cargo that parses arguments

sources.title: Build a Better ls CLI in Rust with Clap

steps.title: Create project and parse args
steps.instructions: Run `cargo new best_ls`, add `clap = { version = "4.5.39", features = ["derive"] }` to Cargo.toml, and define `#[derive(Parser)] struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }` called via `Cli::parse()`. Run `cargo run -- -h` to see the generated help.

targets.caption: Add clap with the derive feature
Derive Parser on the Cli struct

explanations.topic: clap derive feature makes argument parsing easy
Deriving the Parser trait adds parse()
Passing args through cargo run with --
Reading the generated help: usage, arguments, options

hints: Add clap to [dependencies] in Cargo.toml with features = ["derive"], or run `cargo add clap --features derive`.
Import both `std::path::PathBuf` and `clap::Parser` at the top of main.rs.
Put `#[derive(Parser)]` above `struct Cli { path: Option<PathBuf> }`, then `let cli = Cli::parse();` in main.
Run `cargo run -- -h`; the `--` makes -h go to your program instead of cargo.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the "derive" feature, so #[derive(Parser)] fails to compile.
Not importing clap::Parser, giving 'no function named parse' errors.
Running `cargo run -h`, which shows cargo's help instead of the app's.
Using PathBuf without `use std::path::PathBuf`.
Running cargo commands outside the new best_ls directory.
steps.run_command: cargo new best_ls && cd best_ls && cargo run -- -h

steps.title: Add version and about metadata
steps.instructions: Add `#[command(version, about, long_about = "...")]` above the Cli struct. Run `cargo run -- --version` and `cargo run -- -h`.

explanations.topic: #[command(version)] automatically adds a --version flag that reads the version from Cargo.toml
about and long_about descriptions show up in the generated help text
Clap generates the CLI boilerplate so you can focus on program logic

hints: Clap reads extra metadata from an attribute placed on the struct that derives Parser.
Add #[command(version, about, long_about = "...")] directly above your Cli struct.
Make sure clap is added with the derive feature: cargo add clap --features derive.
Pass flags to your program after --, e.g. cargo run -- --version and cargo run -- -h.
common_mistakes: Writing cargo run --version, which prints cargo's version instead of your tool's version.
Putting the #[command(...)] attribute above fn main or another item instead of the Cli struct.
Spelling it longabout or long-about instead of long_about.
Using -h and expecting long_about: -h shows the short about, while --help shows long_about (when about is set without a value, it comes from the Cargo.toml description).

steps.title: Default the path argument
steps.instructions: Set `let path = cli.path.unwrap_or(PathBuf::from("."));` and print it with `path.display()`. Run `cargo run -- some_path` and plain `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Default the path to the current directory
Run with and without a path argument

explanations.topic: cli.path is an Option, so unwrap_or supplies a default
Defaulting to the current directory like ls does
Arguments after -- go to your program, not cargo

hints: cli.path is an Option<PathBuf>. Use unwrap_or to give it a fallback value.
The fallback should be the current directory: PathBuf::from(".").
PathBuf doesn't implement Display. Print it with path.display().
Run `cargo run -- long_path`, then plain `cargo run`. The second run should print a dot.
common_mistakes: Printing the PathBuf directly with {} instead of path.display(), which fails to compile.
Forgetting `use std::path::PathBuf;`.
Running `cargo run long_path` without `--`, so cargo tries to interpret the argument itself.
Using unwrap() instead of unwrap_or, which panics when no path is given.

steps.title: Check path exists with colors
steps.instructions: In src/main.rs use `if let Ok(does_exist) = fs::exists(&path)` to print "Path does not exist" in red via owo-colors (`.red()`), or "error reading directory" on Err. Run `cargo build && ./target/debug/<your-binary> some/bogus/path` to see the red message.

targets.caption: Red message for a bogus path

explanations.topic: fs::exists returns a Result<bool>, checked with if let
owo-colors crate for colored terminal output
cargo build puts the debug executable in target/debug
Err means existence can be neither confirmed nor denied

hints: Use std::fs::exists(&path). It returns Result<bool, io::Error>, so match it with `if let Ok(does_exist) = ...`.
Add owo-colors to Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add owo-colors`), then `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;` so `.red()` works on strings.
Write `println!("{}", "Path does not exist".red());` inside the `else` branch of `if does_exist`.
Handle the Err case with an `else` on the `if let` that prints "error reading directory". Then run with a path that doesn't exist.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use owo_colors::OwoColorize;`, which gives "no method named `red`".
Writing the crate name in Cargo.toml as owo_colors instead of owo-colors.
Calling fs::exists on an older Rust toolchain where it isn't stable (it needs Rust 1.81+). Run `rustup update`.
Treating the result as a bool directly instead of unwrapping the Result with if let Ok(...).
Passing `path` by value and then using it again later, which causes a moved-value error. Pass `&path`.

steps.title: List directory file names
steps.instructions: Write `fn get_files(path: &Path) -> Vec<String>` using `fs::read_dir`, pushing each `file_name()` string. Loop over `get_files(&path)` and print each file, then `cargo run`.

explanations.topic: Defining get_files that returns a Vec<String> to be expanded later
if let Ok with fs::read_dir to handle read errors
file_name().into_string() returns a Result; unwrap_or falls back to "unknown name"
cargo run with no argument defaults to the current directory

hints: Write a function that takes &Path and returns Vec<String>. Start with an empty vector and return it.
Use `if let Ok(read_dir) = fs::read_dir(path)` and loop with `for entry in read_dir`, unwrapping each entry with another `if let Ok(file) = entry`.
Push `file.file_name().into_string().unwrap_or("unknown name".into())` onto the vector.
In main, write `for file in get_files(&path) { println!("{}", file); }` and then run `cargo run`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `use std::fs;` or `use std::path::Path;`, which causes unresolved name errors.
Passing `path` instead of `&path` to get_files, which causes a mismatched types error.
Calling `.to_string()` on the OsString returned by file_name(). Use `.into_string()` and handle its Result.
Declaring the vector without `mut`, so `push` fails to compile.
Placing the loop outside the branch that runs when the path exists, or forgetting to return the vector at the end of the function.

steps.title: Collect file metadata into structs
steps.instructions: Add strum, define `enum EntryType { File, Dir }` deriving `Display` and `struct FileEntry { name, e_type, len_bytes: u64, modified: String }` filled via `fs::metadata` in a `map_data` function. Debug-print the entries with `{:#?}` and `cargo run`.

explanations.topic: Designing a struct to hold file metadata
Using an enum for entry type (`type` is a reserved word)
strum's Display derive turns an enum into a string
fs::metadata returns a Result, so match it with if let Ok
Passing the entry path, not the base path, to metadata
Extracting the mapping into map_data

hints: Add strum (with the derive feature) to Cargo.toml, then define an EntryType enum with File and Dir variants.
Define FileEntry with name: String, e_type: EntryType, len_bytes: u64, modified: String, and derive Debug so you can print it with {:#?}.
Inside the loop, use `if let Ok(meta) = fs::metadata(&file.path())`, then use meta.is_dir() and meta.len() to fill the struct. Leave modified as a placeholder string.
Move that logic into `fn map_data(file: fs::DirEntry, data: &mut Vec<FileEntry>)` and call it from the loop. Then run `cargo run`.
common_mistakes: Passing the base directory path to fs::metadata instead of the entry's own path. Every entry then reports the same metadata.
Naming a field `type`, which is a reserved keyword. Use e_type instead.
Adding strum without the derive feature, or forgetting `use strum::Display`, so #[derive(Display)] fails to compile.
Forgetting #[derive(Debug)] on FileEntry or EntryType, which breaks {:#?} printing.
Treating fs::metadata as returning an Option and writing `if let Some`. It returns a Result, so use `Ok`.

steps.title: Render a colored table
steps.instructions: Add tabled, derive `Tabled` on your file struct, build `Table::new(get_files(&path))` with `Style::rounded()` and column/row colors, rename headers with `#[tabled(rename = ...)]`, and print the table. Run `cargo run`.

targets.caption: Build a table straight from the Vec<FileEntry>
Color the first column bright cyan

explanations.topic: What the tabled crate does: render structs as ASCII tables
Choosing a table Style (rounded)
Targeting columns/rows with modify to add colors
Renaming headers with #[tabled(rename)]

hints: Add tabled to Cargo.toml (cargo add tabled), then derive Tabled on FileEntry alongside Debug.
Replace the print loop with let mut table = Table::new(get_files(&path)); and println!("{}", table).
Use table.with(Style::rounded()) and table.modify(Columns::first(), Color::FG_BRIGHT_CYAN); Columns::one(n) and Rows::first() target other parts.
Above each field add #[tabled(rename = "Name")] etc. to change header text.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to derive Tabled, so Table::new fails to compile.
Every field type (e.g. the EntryType enum) must implement Display for Tabled; missing it causes a compile error.
Importing Style/Color/Columns from wrong module paths (they live under tabled::settings).
Declaring table without mut, so with()/modify() can't be called.
Using a column index beyond the number of fields.

steps.title: Format modified dates with chrono
steps.instructions: Add chrono and in `map_data` convert `meta.modified()` into `DateTime<Utc>` and `.format(...)` it to a string, else an empty string. Run `cargo run` to see the date column.

explanations.topic: Why chrono: std has no date/time formatting
if let Ok / else fallback to an empty string
metadata.modified() returns Result<SystemTime>
Converting SystemTime into DateTime<Utc> with .into()
`mod` is a reserved keyword, so rename the binding
strftime-style format specifiers in .format()

hints: Add chrono under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml (or run `cargo add chrono`), then import it with `use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};`.
meta.modified() returns a Result<SystemTime>. Use `if let Ok(modi) = meta.modified() { ... } else { String::new() }` so the field is always a String.
Inside the Ok branch, convert with `let date: DateTime<Utc> = modi.into();`. The explicit type annotation tells .into() what to produce.
Return `format!("{}", date.format("%a %b %e %Y"))` (any strftime pattern works), then run `cargo run` and check the Modified column.
common_mistakes: Naming the binding `mod`. It is a Rust keyword, so use something like `modi`.
Forgetting the `DateTime<Utc>` type annotation, which leaves .into() unable to infer the target type.
Not importing DateTime and Utc from chrono, which causes 'cannot find type' errors.
Returning a DelayedFormat instead of a String. Wrap it in format!() or call .to_string().
Mismatched branch types, such as returning "" (a &str) in the else branch while the struct field expects a String.
Adding chrono to Cargo.toml in the wrong section instead of under [dependencies].

steps.title: Add a JSON output flag
steps.instructions: Add `#[arg(short, long)] json: bool` to Cli, extract `print_table`, derive `Serialize` on your entry types, and print `serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path))` when `cli.json`. Run `cargo run -- -j`.

targets.caption: New -j/--json boolean flag on the Cli struct
Table rendering extracted into its own function
Serialize the file entries to JSON when --json is set

explanations.topic: #[arg(short, long)] creates -j and --json flags
Using serde + serde_json to serialize structs to JSON
Serialize must be derived on the nested enum too
unwrap_or provides a fallback string on serialization failure

hints: A plain `json: bool` field won't show up as a flag until you annotate it with `#[arg(short, long)]`.
Add `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }` and `serde_json` to Cargo.toml (e.g. `cargo add serde -F derive` and `cargo add serde_json`).
Every type inside FileEntry, including the EntryType enum, needs `#[derive(Serialize)]`.
In main: `if cli.json { println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&get_files(&path)).unwrap_or("cannot parse json".to_string())); } else { print_table(path); }`
common_mistakes: Forgetting `#[arg(short, long)]`, so clap treats `json` as a positional argument instead of a flag.
Adding serde without the `derive` feature, so `#[derive(Serialize)]` fails to compile.
Deriving Serialize on FileEntry but not on EntryType, causing a 'trait Serialize is not implemented' error.
Running `cargo run -j` instead of `cargo run -- -j`, so cargo rather than the program receives the flag.
Passing the result directly to println! without a "{}" format string.
